Session‑based recommendation (SBR) focuses on predicting the next item a user will click within an anonymous, short‑lived session, which precludes the use of long‑term user profiles and thus demands models that can extract rich preference signals from limited interaction sequences.  The seminal work that introduced graph neural networks (GNNs) to this problem modeled each session as a directed item‑transition graph and employed gated graph neural units to learn item embeddings that capture complex, non‑sequential relationships, achieving a marked improvement over pure sequential baselines [S2:0c7e1338a9c7914a3b9a5bdc42b457b3f272160e].  This formulation highlighted two key challenges: (i) the need for accurate item representations that reflect higher‑order transitions, and (ii) the difficulty of deriving reliable session representations when only a few clicks are observed.

Subsequent studies refined the graph‑based paradigm by addressing these challenges from complementary angles.  NISER introduced normalized item and session representations to mitigate the bias caused by varying session lengths and to stabilize GNN propagation, thereby further boosting recommendation accuracy [S2:65b8145199089d484a4d9e0baeb2e1ce9145d6fd].  Star‑GNN proposed a star‑shaped aggregation scheme that separates a central “session node” from peripheral item nodes, enabling more effective fusion of global session context and local item transitions [S2:63f9bc0d97bdfc80b0227415d170941c211acf43].  Recognizing that pairwise item edges ignore higher‑order co‑occurrence patterns, Self‑Supervised Hypergraph Convolutional Networks modeled sessions as hypergraphs, allowing simultaneous learning of multi‑item relations and leveraging self‑supervision to enrich item embeddings [S2:c3ef11a7a8a46f1f193250dd68838cb72b7de0bc].  Global Context Enhanced GNN (GCE‑GNN) extended the session graph with a global item‑transition graph built from all historical sessions, thereby providing subtle cross‑session signals while still preserving session‑specific dynamics [S2:b05a5424d0fce45896b6b8a847cf540a38f556bc].  Temporal Augmented GNN incorporated explicit time stamps into the graph propagation, addressing the drift of user interests over long time spans and enabling the model to weigh recent interactions more heavily [S2:dc3874003319001f276ec752dd427ac338619bf4].

More recent efforts have emphasized collaborative and contextual supervision across sessions.  Collaborative Graph Learning introduced inter‑session item correlations as additional supervision signals, arguing that the neglect of such correlations in earlier GNN‑based SBR models limits representation learning; the proposed framework jointly optimizes intra‑session graph learning and inter‑session collaborative signals [S2:0552e5f53bb30cda3e838e7e136490790a6527f8].  A multi‑behavior extension further enriched the session graph by integrating heterogeneous user actions (e.g., clicks, likes, purchases) into a unified GNN, demonstrating that leveraging multiple behavior types can capture more nuanced user intent [S2:3a0b49179ce8f3ed5fe0d104f7c3817f7449770c].  Building on these ideas, CCT‑GNN combined collaborative category information with time‑aware graph convolutions, explicitly modeling both item categories and temporal dynamics to improve recommendation quality in highly dynamic environments [S2:bb4e06efa0d947fb8c7a63fa154ca53991ae9b66].

A broader synthesis of these developments is provided by a recent survey that categorizes GNN‑based recommender systems into knowledge‑aware, collaborative, sequential, and hybrid streams, and outlines future research directions such as explainability, scalability, and integration of large‑language models [S2:a669fc2d44fe5c49116a603f10d04a353468e190].  Collectively, the literature demonstrates a clear trajectory: from representing a single session as a simple graph, to enriching graph structures with normalization, star‑shaped aggregation, hypergraph modeling, global context, temporal signals, collaborative supervision, and multi‑behavior information.  Despite these advances, open challenges remain, including efficient handling of ever‑growing session graphs, real‑time adaptation to rapid interest drift, and unified frameworks that can simultaneously exploit high‑order relations, temporal dynamics, and heterogeneous behaviors.
